content.content:
# Write a reviewer rule

A script rule (lawcheck docs concepts) can find `console.log` in a file. It cannot tell whether the message of `new Error('failed')` tells the caller what to do next. A reviewer rule (lawcheck docs concepts) can tell. With a reviewer rule, a language model reads each file against a rule (lawcheck docs concepts) you write in plain words. That model is the reviewer.

You end with a reviewer rule that judges `src/core/`. Lawcheck records the verdict (lawcheck docs concepts) of the reviewer in `.lawcheck/verdicts`. A later `lawcheck check` without `--review` reads that verdict in place of a call to the model.

The outputs below come from a repository whose `main` holds the `.lawcheck/` that `lawcheck init` makes. Its law (lawcheck docs concepts) has the type (lawcheck docs concepts) `library` that [Put the rule in the law](#_2-put-the-rule-in-the-law) shows, without the rule. On a branch made from `main`, you added `src/core/refund.ts`:

```ts
export function refund(paid: boolean): number {
  if (!paid) throw new Error('failed');
  return 1;
}
```

A test server that answers as Ollama does gave the answers below. A real model words its findings (lawcheck docs concepts) in its own way.

## 1. Write the rule file

`init` makes no `rules/` folder. Create it with `mkdir -p .lawcheck/rules`, then write the file `.lawcheck/rules/clear-errors.md`. It says what must hold, what to report, and what does not count:

```text
Every error message a caller can see says what happened and what the caller can do next.

Report each thrown error or returned error message that leaves one of the two out. A message logged for developers is not such a message.
```

The reviewer receives this text, the rule's `why` and the file it judges.

## 2. Put the rule in the law

Give the rule a `why`. List the rule on the type. The reviewer may need another file beside the file it judges, such as a catalogue of messages. In that case, list the file under the `context` key of the rule (Reviewer rules (lawcheck docs reviewer-rules)). Write `.lawcheck/law.yaml`:

```yaml
lawcheck: 0.1.0

rules:
  clear-errors:
    why: An error a caller sees says what happened and what to do next.

types:
  library:
    about: Code the commands call.
    paths: ["src/core/**"]
    rules: [clear-errors]
```

## 3. Choose a reviewer

| You have | `provider` | Key |
|---|---|---|
| an API key of Anthropic, OpenAI or Google | `anthropic`, `openai` or `google` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` in the environment |
| a model on your own machine, served by Ollama | `ollama` | none |
| another server that answers chat completions as OpenAI does | `openai-compatible`, with its address in `LAWCHECK_REVIEWER_ENDPOINT` | `LAWCHECK_REVIEWER_KEY` in the environment, when the server needs a key |
| Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or Copilot CLI, signed in | `claude-code`, `codex`, `gemini-cli` or `copilot-cli` | the program's own sign-in |

These steps use Ollama. Lawcheck calls it on `localhost:11434`, or at the address in `LAWCHECK_REVIEWER_ENDPOINT`. Create `.lawcheck/config.yaml`, with the name of a model the server has pulled:

```yaml
reviewer:
  provider: ollama
  model: your-model-id
```

A key goes in the environment, because Lawcheck refuses a key in this file with `config-invalid` (lawcheck docs codes). Reviewers and keys (lawcheck docs providers) has every provider and its keys.

## 4. Check that the reviewer answers

```text
$ lawcheck doctor --reviewer
```

`doctor` sends the reviewer one small request. The last line of its output is:

```output
ok  reviewer  1 reviewer rule; ollama answered a test call
```

## 5. See what the change needs

```text
$ lawcheck check --base main
```

```output
lawcheck: FAIL  1 error in 4 changed files (against main)
note: the law changed in this change; lawcheck check --full --base main shows what it finds in the rest of the code
note: this change edits the law that judges it: adds the rule clear-errors; adds .lawcheck/rules/clear-errors.md; adds .lawcheck/config.yaml

src/core/refund.ts  error[not-reviewed]  clear-errors has no verdict for this content
  why:  a reviewer rule says nothing about content it has not judged

next: lawcheck check --review --base main  (1 reviewer call)
```

`lawcheck check` without `--review` judges the change (lawcheck docs concepts). It calls no model. Its `next:` line counts the calls a review would make.

## 6. See the cost of a try

```text
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts --dry-run
```

```output
lawcheck: try clear-errors (reviewer rule, enforced)  dry run: 1 reviewer call, none made

src/core/refund.ts  1 call, a prompt of 1814 characters
```

Each file you name costs one call. `--times 2` makes it two calls.

## 7. Try the rule on the file

`try` sends the prompt that `check --review` would send. It records nothing:

```text
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts
```

```output
lawcheck: 1 reviewer call to ollama
lawcheck: try clear-errors (reviewer rule, enforced)  1 finding in 1 of 1 file, 1 reviewer call

src/core/refund.ts:2  error[clear-errors]  the message says neither what happened nor what to do next
  why:  An error a caller sees says what happened and what to do next.
```

## 8. Ask the same question twice

```text
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts --times 2
```

```output
lawcheck: 2 reviewer calls to ollama
lawcheck: try clear-errors (reviewer rule, enforced)  2 answers for 1 file: 2 fail, 0 pass, 2 reviewer calls

src/core/refund.ts  answer 1 of 2: fail
src/core/refund.ts:2  error[clear-errors]  the message says neither what happened nor what to do next
  why:  An error a caller sees says what happened and what to do next.
src/core/refund.ts  answer 2 of 2: fail
src/core/refund.ts:2  error[clear-errors]  the message says neither what happened nor what to do next
```

Two answers that differ mean that the rule allows two readings. Reword the rule file. Ask again until the answers agree.

## 9. Fix the file

Make the message say what happened and what to do:

```ts
export function refund(paid: boolean): number {
  if (!paid) throw new Error('The order is not paid yet; take the payment before a refund.');
  return 1;
}
```

## 10. Review the change

```text
$ lawcheck check --review --base main
```

```output
lawcheck: 1 reviewer call to ollama
lawcheck: PASS  4 changed files (against main), 1 reviewer call
note: the law changed in this change; lawcheck check --full --base main shows what it finds in the rest of the code
note: this change edits the law that judges it: adds the rule clear-errors; adds .lawcheck/rules/clear-errors.md; adds .lawcheck/config.yaml
```

Lawcheck wrote the pass to `.lawcheck/verdicts`. It wrote `.lawcheck/.gitattributes` beside it. With that file, git merges the passes of two branches without a conflict.

## 11. Commit the verdicts

Commit the passes with the change. The page leaves out the lines that git prints:

```text
$ git add .lawcheck src
$ git commit -m "Errors of the library say what to do next"
```

## 12. Check as CI does

```text
$ lawcheck check --base main
```

```output
lawcheck: PASS  6 changed files (against main)
note: the law changed in this change; lawcheck check --full --base main shows what it finds in the rest of the code
note: this change edits the law that judges it: adds the rule clear-errors; adds .lawcheck/rules/clear-errors.md; adds .lawcheck/config.yaml
```

A plain check (lawcheck docs concepts) reads the pass from `.lawcheck/verdicts`. It calls no model. A CI job runs the same plain check with no key (CI and git hooks (lawcheck docs ci)).

## If it goes wrong

- Lawcheck prints `reviewer-unreachable` (lawcheck docs codes): the server is down, the key is wrong, or the program is not signed in. The message names the cause. Fix the cause and run the same command again. `check --review` keeps the answers it got before the failure, so the second run asks the reviewer only about the files it has no answer for.
- The reviewer failed a file you believe is right. Lawcheck keeps the fail on this machine. It shows the fail again without a call, until the file or the rule changes. With `--again`, Lawcheck asks the reviewer once more: `lawcheck check --review --again --base main`.
- Lawcheck prints `too-large-to-review` (lawcheck docs codes): the prompt of a file holds more characters than the setting `reviewer.max_chars` allows. Its default is 50,000. Lawcheck never sends such a prompt. Split the file, or raise `max_chars` in `.lawcheck/config.yaml`.
- Lawcheck prints `reviewer-bad-answer` (lawcheck docs codes): the model gave no verdict twice. Reword the rule file, or try another model.
- Lawcheck prints `too-many-reviews` (lawcheck docs codes): the run needs more calls than the setting `reviewer.max_calls` allows (100 by default). Lawcheck then makes none of them. A slow check (lawcheck docs slow-check) shows how to cap the calls.
- Lawcheck keeps every recorded pass after you change the model or the provider. It records a pass under a key made from the file and the rule. The key holds no provider and no model. Check the new setup with `lawcheck doctor --reviewer`.

Next: Bring a law into an existing repository (lawcheck docs adopt-in-an-existing-repository)
# Reviewer rules

A reviewer rule (lawcheck docs concepts) is a rule in prose that a language model judges. That model is the reviewer. For example, the rule `clear-errors` below asks that each error a caller sees says what to do next. The reviewer reads the error messages of a file and reports each one that names no next action.

## The rule file

Each reviewer rule has its file `.lawcheck/rules/<id>.md`. The file holds your instruction to the reviewer, in plain prose or Markdown. The law (lawcheck docs concepts) holds the rule's `why`, `status` and `context` (`lawcheck docs law`). The YAML key `context` lists files that Lawcheck sends the reviewer with each file that the reviewer judges for this rule. Such a file can be a page of your error codes:

```yaml
lawcheck: 0.1.0

rules:
  clear-errors:
    why: An error a caller sees says what happened and what to do next.
    context: ["docs/errors.md"]
```

A good rule file says what must hold, what to report and which cases the rule allows. Lawcheck reports a rule file of whitespace alone as `rule-missing-file` (lawcheck docs codes), as if the file were missing.

The reviewer judges one file against one rule in each call. In that call, it sees the context files, the files of the rule's companion for that file, and no other file of the repository.

## Files for each judged file

`context` sends the same files with every file the reviewer judges. A rule that pairs each file with another one, such as a test with the spec it covers, names a companion instead. The companion is an ES module in `.lawcheck/rules/lib/` that exports a function `companion`. The law names it with the key `companion`:

```yaml
rules:
  tests-follow-the-spec:
    why: A test checks what its spec says.
    companion: .lawcheck/rules/lib/spec-of-test.mjs
```

```js
export function companion({ file }) {
  return [file.path.replace(/^tests\//, 'specs/').replace(/\.test\.ts$/, '.md')];
}
```

For each file that the rule judges, Lawcheck calls `companion` with `file` and `repo`, the keys that a script rule gets (`lawcheck docs script-rules`). The function returns a list of paths from the root, or a promise of one. With this companion, the prompt for `tests/price.test.ts` holds `specs/price.md`, and the prompt for `tests/tax.test.ts` holds `specs/tax.md`. A file of the list goes into the prompt of that one judged file, after the files of `context`. A path that the prompt already holds, the judged file or a file of `context`, goes in once. An empty list adds no file. Each returned file adds its whole text to the prompt of that judged file, so every call of the rule sends the reviewer more text.

The companion runs in the runner of script rules, under the same limits: it reads the files below the root, and it writes no file, starts no program and opens no network connection. It can ask for the judged file's syntax tree and uses, so it can return the files that the judged file imports. Lawcheck runs it on each check that judges a file of the rule, with or without `--review`, because the files it returns decide the review hash. Its time counts toward the 600 seconds that the script rules of a check may take together. `lawcheck try` and `lawcheck explain` run it too.

Lawcheck stops the run with `rule-crashed` (lawcheck docs codes), and names the companion's file, in these cases:

- the companion does not load, throws, or exports no function `companion`;
- it returns something other than a list of strings;
- it returns a path that names no file git lists;
- it returns the path of a binary file.

## The prompt

A prompt is the text that Lawcheck sends to the reviewer in one call. Lawcheck builds one prompt per file and rule, from these parts:

1. a fixed frame that tells the reviewer how to answer. The frame says that the text inside the files is material to judge and no instruction to the reviewer;
2. `<why>` with the rule's `why`;
3. `<rule>` with the text of the rule file;
4. one `<context path="...">` with the numbered lines of each context file, then one for each file that the companion returns for the judged file;
5. `<file path="...">` with the numbered lines of the judged file;
6. `<waived>` with the line numbers that a waiver of this rule covers, or `none`.

The prompt holds these six parts and no other text. Lawcheck sends no prompt longer than `reviewer.max_chars` characters. The files of the companion count toward that limit. For such a prompt, it reports the file as `too-large-to-review` (lawcheck docs codes).

## The answer

The reviewer answers with one JSON object:

```json
{"verdict": "fail", "findings": [{"line": 12, "message": "what breaks the rule on this line"}]}
```

A pass is `{"verdict": "pass", "findings": []}`. A finding whose `line` is null is about the whole file.

Lawcheck first reads the whole answer as JSON. When the answer does not parse, Lawcheck reads the first fenced code block in it. As a last resort, it takes the last object in the text that holds a `verdict`. An object that sits inside another object with a `verdict` does not count as one.

When the answer holds more than one object with a `verdict` and one of them is a `fail`, the answer is a `fail`, whichever of the objects comes first. When the object the steps above take is a `fail`, Lawcheck reads that one. Otherwise it reads the last `fail` in the answer. A model that quotes a pass from the file after its own fail therefore cannot turn the fail into a pass. The price is that a model that quotes a fail in a sentence after a pass makes the file fail, with the findings of the quoted fail. When that fail is itself a bad answer, such as a fail with no finding, the answer is bad.

An answer is bad when Lawcheck finds in it no object with a `verdict` of `pass` or `fail`. An object with such a verdict is bad in these cases:

- a pass with findings;
- a fail without a finding;
- `findings` that is no list, or a finding that is no object;
- a finding with no message;
- a finding with a line outside the file.

A pass is bad too when the answer also holds an object whose `verdict` is neither `pass` nor `fail`, such as `"Fail"`, or an object with the key `verdict` twice. JSON keeps the last of two equal keys, so `{"verdict": "fail", ..., "verdict": "pass"}` would read as a pass. A pass is bad as well when the answer holds a `"verdict": "fail"` outside every object that parses, such as a fail with a trailing comma: the fail may be the real verdict.

After a bad answer, Lawcheck asks the reviewer once more, if the setting `reviewer.max_calls` leaves room for one more request ([Asking the reviewer](#asking-the-reviewer)). A second bad answer stops the run with `reviewer-bad-answer` (lawcheck docs codes). The run stops with the same code after one bad answer when `reviewer.max_calls` leaves no room.

From a good answer, Lawcheck makes each finding a finding of the rule, at its line or on the whole file. Lawcheck drops each finding on a waived line. When a fail keeps no finding after that, Lawcheck counts the answer as a pass.

## Verdicts

A verdict (lawcheck docs concepts) is the reviewer's answer, pass or fail, for one file and one rule. Lawcheck records each pass as a line of `.lawcheck/verdicts`. A line holds the review hash and the rule id. When the law names signers, the line also holds the signer's name and a signature ([Signed passes](#signed-passes)). The review hash is a hash of these parts:

- the frame;
- the rule id, its `why` and the text of the rule file;
- the path and text of each context file, and of each file that the companion returned;
- the path and text of the companion's module;
- the path and text of the judged file;
- the waived lines that the prompt names.

A change to any of these parts gives a new review hash. Lawcheck then finds no pass for the file and rule. The file needs a new review. A new waiver changes the review hash, because the waiver is part of the text of the file. A change to `specs/price.md` gives a new review hash to `tests/price.test.ts` alone. A change to the companion's module gives one to every file of the rule. A module that the companion imports is not part of the review hash: a change to it gives a new one only to the files whose returned files it changes.

Lawcheck leaves the rule's `status`, the provider, the model and the other settings out of the review hash. A recorded pass stays valid when you change any of them.

In a type with `waivers: false`, Lawcheck reads a waiver marker as plain text. The prompt names no waived line. The reviewer judges the line that the marker would cover, as it judges any other line. The file then gets a new review hash, since the waived lines are part of it. A pass that Lawcheck recorded while the type read the waiver no longer matches the file. Two changes of the law cause that:

- the file's type sets `waivers: false` after the review;
- a change of the law moves the file into a type with `waivers: false`.

Lawcheck keeps the lines of `.lawcheck/verdicts` sorted. Commit this file. A plain `lawcheck check` (lawcheck docs concepts) reads it and calls no reviewer for a file and rule that have a pass there. A CI job then needs no API key.

Lawcheck writes `verdicts merge=union` into `.lawcheck/.gitattributes`. With that line, git merges `.lawcheck/verdicts` without a conflict when two branches both add lines to it.

Lawcheck holds a lock in `.lawcheck/.local/` while it writes `.lawcheck/verdicts`. When two runs write at once, the file ends with the passes of both.

## Signed passes

A person who can push a branch can write a line into `.lawcheck/verdicts`. The review hash holds nothing secret, so a pull request can add passes for its own files. A reviewer that answers pass to everything records passes too. Under a law without signers, a check counts every such line as a review.

When the law names signers, a pass counts only when a signer of the law signed it. Make a signing key on the machine, or in the job, that records the reviews. This command prints a new key on its first line and the key's public key on its second:

```sh
node -e "const k = require('node:crypto').generateKeyPairSync('ed25519'); console.log(k.privateKey.export({ format: 'jwk' }).d); console.log(k.publicKey.export({ format: 'jwk' }).x)"
```

Keep the first line secret, and set it as `LAWCHECK_SIGNING_KEY` where you run `lawcheck check --review`. Lawcheck writes it as `[key]` wherever it would show it, and it gives the variable to no reviewer program. Then name the signer with the second line in `.lawcheck/law.yaml`:

```yaml
signers:
  alice: PMAs5_zHsaCR2qES93_G3eFFNwRUCQm6Qz8l5_SnIw8
```

Under a law with `signers`, a review works this way:

- `lawcheck check --review` signs each pass it records with the key in `LAWCHECK_SIGNING_KEY`. When the variable is not set, or holds the key of no signer of the law, the run stops with `not-a-signer` (lawcheck docs codes) before its first call.
- A signed line holds the review hash, the rule id, the signer's name and the signature: `<hash> <rule> <signer> <signature>`. The signature is Ed25519 over the text `lawcheck-signed-pass/1 <hash> <rule>`, in base64url.
- A pass counts when its line names a signer of the law and that signer's key verifies the signature. Lawcheck reports a file with no such line as `not-reviewed`. When the file and rule have a line that does not count, the message says `has a pass for this content that no signer of the law signed`.
- `--review` asks the reviewer again about each pass that does not count. It signs the answers it gets, and never a line the file already held.

A law without `signers` reads and writes `.lawcheck/verdicts` without signatures. It counts a signed line as a pass too.

A signature proves that someone whose key the law names recorded the pass. A signer can run any reviewer, so name as signers only the people and the jobs that you trust with a review. A review of a pull request asks the reviewer that its `.lawcheck/config.yaml` names, with the Lawcheck that its `package.json` installs, so a signer reads both first. A job in CI runs the workflow of the branch it reviews, so anyone who can push a branch can make a job that holds the key sign any pass. A pull request from a fork gets no secret, so it cannot. In CI, the second check of the workflow reads the law of the base, so the signers of the base decide (The job trusts the verdicts (lawcheck docs ci)).

When you add `signers` to a law, the passes already in the file carry no signature, and they stop counting. A plain check judges the changed files, so each file needs one signed review when it next changes. `lawcheck check --strict --review` asks about every file at once. Lawcheck 0.1.0-alpha.4 and older stop on a law with `signers` with `law-invalid`, so every checkout and every job needs a later version first.

## The failure cache

Lawcheck keeps each failed review on this machine, in `.lawcheck/.local/failures/<hash>.json`. The name of that file is the review hash. Git ignores every file in `.lawcheck/.local/`, because the folder holds a `.gitignore` of its own. A later run with the same review hash shows the cached findings and calls no reviewer. When a later review of that hash passes, Lawcheck removes the failure file.

## The state of a review

A rule binds a file when the file's type, or a type above it, lists the rule. For each judged file and each reviewer rule that binds it, Lawcheck takes the first of these states that applies:

1. `.lawcheck/verdicts` holds a line with the review hash of the file and rule: a pass, and Lawcheck shows nothing;
2. the failure cache holds a fail: Lawcheck shows its findings again, with or without `--review`;
3. the prompt holds more than `reviewer.max_chars` characters: `too-large-to-review`;
4. otherwise: `not-reviewed`.

`not-reviewed` and `too-large-to-review` are errors in the change (lawcheck docs concepts) for a rule whose `status` is `enforced`. The two are warnings in these cases:

- for a rule whose `status` is `advisory`;
- in debt (lawcheck docs concepts);
- for files you name on the command line.

`lawcheck explain <path>` shows this state for each reviewer rule of a file.

## Asking the reviewer

```text
$ lawcheck check --review --base main
$ lawcheck check --review --again --base main
$ lawcheck check --review --max-calls 3 --base main
```

- With `--review`, Lawcheck asks the reviewer about each file and rule that have neither a pass in `.lawcheck/verdicts` nor a cached failure. Lawcheck records each new pass and caches each new failure.
- With `--again`, Lawcheck asks the reviewer again about each review whose failure the cache holds.
- `--max-calls <n>` replaces `reviewer.max_calls` for one run.

`reviewer.max_calls` sets the most requests that one run may send to the reviewer. A request that Lawcheck sends again counts as one more request. A run that needs more requests than that limit sends none. It stops with `too-many-reviews` (lawcheck docs codes).

Without `--review`, `lawcheck check` sends no request to a reviewer. `lawcheck doctor` opens no connection to one either, with one exception: when the provider is `ollama` and the law holds a reviewer rule, it sends `GET <address>/api/version` to the server, with a time limit of 5 seconds. The request carries no prompt and no text of your repository. `lawcheck doctor --reviewer` sends a test prompt (Reviewers and keys (lawcheck docs providers)).

A request that fails stops the run with `reviewer-unreachable` (lawcheck docs codes). The passes that the run recorded before that request stay in `.lawcheck/verdicts`. When you run the same command again, Lawcheck asks the reviewer only about the reviews still missing.

## Trying a reviewer rule

`lawcheck try` sends the reviewer the files you name, with the prompt that `lawcheck check --review` would send. `try` records no pass and caches no failure.

```text
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts --dry-run
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts --times 3
```

- `--dry-run` makes no call. It prints the calls that the run would make, with the size of each prompt. Each file costs one call. Start with `--dry-run` to see how many calls a real run makes.
- `--times <n>` sends each file to the reviewer n times. The answers show whether the reviewer judges the file the same way each time.
- `--max-calls <n>` sets the limit of requests for the run, as it does for `check`.

For a reviewer rule, `lawcheck try` takes the files one by one, by name. It stops with `usage` (lawcheck docs codes) on a folder, on a pattern and when you name no file.

Reviewers and keys (lawcheck docs providers) says how to set a reviewer up.

  if (!paid) throw new Error('failed');

```

A test server that answers as Ollama does gave the answers below. A real model words its findings (lawcheck docs concepts) in its own way.

## 1. Write the rule file

`init` makes no `rules/` folder. Create it with `mkdir -p .lawcheck/rules`, then write the file `.lawcheck/rules/clear-errors.md`. It says what must hold, what to report, and what does not count:

```text
Every error message a caller can see says what happened and what the caller can do next.

Report each thrown error or returned error message that leaves one of the two out. A message logged for developers is not such a message.
```

The reviewer receives this text, the rule's `why` and the file it judges.

## 2. Put the rule in the law

Give the rule a `why`. List the rule on the type. The reviewer may need another file beside the file it judges, such as a catalogue of messages. In that case, list the file under the `context` key of the rule (Reviewer rules (lawcheck docs reviewer-rules)). Write `.lawcheck/law.yaml`:

lawcheck: 0.1.0

rules:
  clear-errors:
    why: An error a caller sees says what happened and what to do next.

    about: Code the commands call.
    paths: ["src/core/**"]

```

# Reviewer rules

A reviewer rule (lawcheck docs concepts) is a rule in prose that a language model judges. That model is the reviewer. For example, the rule `clear-errors` below asks that each error a caller sees says what to do next. The reviewer reads the error messages of a file and reports each one that names no next action.

## The rule file

Each reviewer rule has its file `.lawcheck/rules/<id>.md`. The file holds your instruction to the reviewer, in plain prose or Markdown. The law (lawcheck docs concepts) holds the rule's `why`, `status` and `context` (`lawcheck docs law`). The YAML key `context` lists files that Lawcheck sends the reviewer with each file that the reviewer judges for this rule. Such a file can be a page of your error codes:

```yaml
lawcheck: 0.1.0

rules:
  clear-errors:
    why: An error a caller sees says what happened and what to do next.
    context: ["docs/errors.md"]
```

A good rule file says what must hold, what to report and which cases the rule allows. Lawcheck reports a rule file of whitespace alone as `rule-missing-file` (lawcheck docs codes), as if the file were missing.

The reviewer judges one file against one rule in each call. In that call, it sees the context files, the files of the rule's companion for that file, and no other file of the repository.

## Files for each judged file

`context` sends the same files with every file the reviewer judges. A rule that pairs each file with another one, such as a test with the spec it covers, names a companion instead. The companion is an ES module in `.lawcheck/rules/lib/` that exports a function `companion`. The law names it with the key `companion`:

```yaml
rules:
  tests-follow-the-spec:
    why: A test checks what its spec says.
    companion: .lawcheck/rules/lib/spec-of-test.mjs
```

```js
export function companion({ file }) {
  return [file.path.replace(/^tests\//, 'specs/').replace(/\.test\.ts$/, '.md')];
}
```

For each file that the rule judges, Lawcheck calls `companion` with `file` and `repo`, the keys that a script rule gets (`lawcheck docs script-rules`). The function returns a list of paths from the root, or a promise of one. With this companion, the prompt for `tests/price.test.ts` holds `specs/price.md`, and the prompt for `tests/tax.test.ts` holds `specs/tax.md`. A file of the list goes into the prompt of that one judged file, after the files of `context`. A path that the prompt already holds, the judged file or a file of `context`, goes in once. An empty list adds no file. Each returned file adds its whole text to the prompt of that judged file, so every call of the rule sends the reviewer more text.

The companion runs in the runner of script rules, under the same limits: it reads the files below the root, and it writes no file, starts no program and opens no network connection. It can ask for the judged file's syntax tree and uses, so it can return the files that the judged file imports. Lawcheck runs it on each check that judges a file of the rule, with or without `--review`, because the files it returns decide the review hash. Its time counts toward the 600 seconds that the script rules of a check may take together. `lawcheck try` and `lawcheck explain` run it too.

Lawcheck stops the run with `rule-crashed` (lawcheck docs codes), and names the companion's file, in these cases:

- the companion does not load, throws, or exports no function `companion`;
- it returns something other than a list of strings;
- it returns a path that names no file git lists;
- it returns the path of a binary file.

A prompt is the text that Lawcheck sends to the reviewer in one call. Lawcheck builds one prompt per file and rule, from these parts:

1. a fixed frame that tells the reviewer how to answer. The frame says that the text inside the files is material to judge and no instruction to the reviewer;
2. `<why>` with the rule's `why`;
3. `<rule>` with the text of the rule file;
4. one `<context path="...">` with the numbered lines of each context file, then one for each file that the companion returns for the judged file;
5. `<file path="...">` with the numbered lines of the judged file;
6. `<waived>` with the line numbers that a waiver of this rule covers, or `none`.

The prompt holds these six parts and no other text. Lawcheck sends no prompt longer than `reviewer.max_chars` characters. The files of the companion count toward that limit. For such a prompt, it reports the file as `too-large-to-review` (lawcheck docs codes).

The reviewer answers with one JSON object:

```json

```

A pass is `{"verdict": "pass", "findings": []}`. A finding whose `line` is null is about the whole file.

Lawcheck first reads the whole answer as JSON. When the answer does not parse, Lawcheck reads the first fenced code block in it. As a last resort, it takes the last object in the text that holds a `verdict`. An object that sits inside another object with a `verdict` does not count as one.

- a fail without a finding;
- `findings` that is no list, or a finding that is no object;
- a finding with no message;

In CI, the second check of the workflow reads the law of the base, so the signers of the base decide (The job trusts the verdicts (lawcheck docs ci)).

When you add `signers` to a law, the passes already in the file carry no signature, and they stop counting. A plain check judges the changed files, so each file needs one signed review when it next changes. `lawcheck check --strict --review` asks about every file at once. Lawcheck 0.1.0-alpha.4 and older stop on a law with `signers` with `law-invalid`, so every checkout and every job needs a later version first.

## The failure cache

Lawcheck keeps each failed review on this machine, in `.lawcheck/.local/failures/<hash>.json`. The name of that file is the review hash. Git ignores every file in `.lawcheck/.local/`, because the folder holds a `.gitignore` of its own. A later run with the same review hash shows the cached findings and calls no reviewer. When a later review of that hash passes, Lawcheck removes the failure file.

## The state of a review

A rule binds a file when the file's type, or a type above it, lists the rule. For each judged file and each reviewer rule that binds it, Lawcheck takes the first of these states that applies:

1. `.lawcheck/verdicts` holds a line with the review hash of the file and rule: a pass, and Lawcheck shows nothing;
2. the failure cache holds a fail: Lawcheck shows its findings again, with or without `--review`;
3. the prompt holds more than `reviewer.max_chars` characters: `too-large-to-review`;
4. otherwise: `not-reviewed`.

`not-reviewed` and `too-large-to-review` are errors in the change (lawcheck docs concepts) for a rule whose `status` is `enforced`. The two are warnings in these cases:

- for a rule whose `status` is `advisory`;
- in debt (lawcheck docs concepts);
- for files you name on the command line.

`lawcheck explain <path>` shows this state for each reviewer rule of a file.

## Asking the reviewer

```text
$ lawcheck check --review --base main
$ lawcheck check --review --again --base main
$ lawcheck check --review --max-calls 3 --base main
```

- With `--review`, Lawcheck asks the reviewer about each file and rule that have neither a pass in `.lawcheck/verdicts` nor a cached failure. Lawcheck records each new pass and caches each new failure.
- With `--again`, Lawcheck asks the reviewer again about each review whose failure the cache holds.
- `--max-calls <n>` replaces `reviewer.max_calls` for one run.

`reviewer.max_calls` sets the most requests that one run may send to the reviewer. A request that Lawcheck sends again counts as one more request. A run that needs more requests than that limit sends none. It stops with `too-many-reviews` (lawcheck docs codes).

Without `--review`, `lawcheck check` sends no request to a reviewer. `lawcheck doctor` opens no connection to one either, with one exception: when the provider is `ollama` and the law holds a reviewer rule, it sends `GET <address>/api/version` to the server, with a time limit of 5 seconds. The request carries no prompt and no text of your repository. `lawcheck doctor --reviewer` sends a test prompt (Reviewers and keys (lawcheck docs providers)).

A request that fails stops the run with `reviewer-unreachable` (lawcheck docs codes). The passes that the run recorded before that request stay in `.lawcheck/verdicts`. When you run the same command again, Lawcheck asks the reviewer only about the reviews still missing.

## Trying a reviewer rule

`lawcheck try` sends the reviewer the files you name, with the prompt that `lawcheck check --review` would send. `try` records no pass and caches no failure.

```text
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts --dry-run
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts
$ lawcheck try clear-errors src/core/refund.ts --times 3
```

- `--dry-run` makes no call. It prints the calls that the run would make, with the size of each prompt. Each file costs one call. Start with `--dry-run` to see how many calls a real run makes.
- `--times <n>` sends each file to the reviewer n times. The answers show whether the reviewer judges the file the same way each time.
- `--max-calls <n>` sets the limit of requests for the run, as it does for `check`.

For a reviewer rule, `lawcheck try` takes the files one by one, by name. It stops with `usage` (lawcheck docs codes) on a folder, on a pattern and when you name no file.

Reviewers and keys (lawcheck docs providers) says how to set a reviewer up.
